overview: Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara of Jainism, is a revered figure believed to have lived approximately 2,500 years ago. He was born in Varanasi, in the Ikshvaku dynasty, to King Ashvasena and Queen Vamadevi. Parshvanatha is credited with re-establishing the fourfold restraint (Chaturyam), which consists of non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possession. His teachings laid the foundation for Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, who would later expand upon these principles. Parshvanatha renounced worldly life at the age of 30 and attained Kevala Jnana (omniscience) after 84 days of intense meditation. He is often depicted with a serpent hood, symbolizing the protection he received from the serpent deity Dharanendra during his penance.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sutra
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabahu
primary_sources.translation: Parshvanatha was the son of King Ashvasena in Varanasi.
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa Sutra is a revered Jain text that provides biographies of the Tirthankaras, including Parshvanatha.

misconceptions.myth: Parshvanatha introduced the concept of non-violence in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: While Parshvanatha emphasized non-violence, this principle was foundational to Jain philosophy long before his time.
